## About

Leonel A. Regalado Cardoso is a Ph.D. candidate in the Department of Agricultural and
Applied Economics at Texas Tech University (expected Spring 2027) and a Research Assistant
at the Free Market Institute. He is also a Graduate Instructor in the Area of Energy
Commerce & Business Economics at the Rawls College of Business. He holds an M.S. in
Agricultural and Applied Economics from Texas Tech (2025), a B.A. in Economics with a minor
in Finance from Universidad Francisco Marroquín in Guatemala (2023), and a Postgraduate
Certificate in Money, Banking, and Central Banking from the University of Buckingham (2022).

His research sits at the intersection of migration, entrepreneurship, and political economy,
with a focus on how institutions, policy environments, and economic incentives shape
individual behavior and long-run development outcomes. Regional interests include Latin
America (especially Guatemala and Cuba) and Europe.

Contact: lregalad@ttu.edu
CV: https://leoregalado.com/cv.pdf
ORCID: https://orcid.org/0009-0008-3915-8995
GitHub: https://github.com/leoregalado17
LinkedIn: https://www.linkedin.com/in/leonel-regalado/

## Research Focus

Migration, entrepreneurship, and political economy. Core themes:
- Emigration and institutional change in origin countries
- Immigration and institutional quality in destination countries
- Property rights, corruption, and entrepreneurial activity
- Fiscal rules and debt constraints in emerging economies
- Ideology and economic freedom over the long run
- Entrepreneurial elites, exile, and business formation

Empirical methods: synthetic control, difference-in-differences (including
Callaway–Sant'Anna staggered-adoption estimators), panel data with fixed and random
effects, nonlinear/quadratic specifications. Primary data sources: Economic Freedom of the
World (EFW) index, Global Entrepreneurship Monitor (GEM), World Bank Group Entrepreneurship
Survey, World Bank governance indicators, and hand-collected historical business records.

---

## Peer-Reviewed Publications

### Syrian refugees and the resilience of European economic freedom: Evidence from Austria, Germany, and Sweden
Journal: Journal of Comparative Economics (Forthcoming)
With: Benjamin Powell
PDF: https://leoregalado.com/publications/Powell_Regalado_Syrian_Refugees_European_Economic_Freedom_2026.pdf
Summary: The Syrian civil war sent more than a million refugees to Europe, concentrated in
a few destinations: by 2022 Germany hosted 612,000 Syrians, Sweden 232,000, and Austria
77,000 (2.2% of Sweden's population). The paper tests the "new economic case for
immigration restrictions" — the claim that migrants from countries with poor institutions
erode institutions where they settle — using synthetic controls for each destination's
Economic Freedom of the World (EFW) score, built from European countries that received few
Syrian refugees, plus a stacked analysis across the three. Overall EFW fell by more than
its synthetic counterpart in every post-treatment year, but the gaps are small (about 0.11
points on average) and not significant in 7 of 9 years (joint p-value = 0.106). The Legal
System and Property Rights area (EFW Area 2) shows a widening decline, driven by Germany
and Sweden.
Scope: Three destination countries (Austria, Germany, Sweden); EFW outcomes only. The
paper reports TWO findings: no robust evidence of a large negative effect on OVERALL
economic freedom, and SUGGESTIVE evidence of a negative effect on Germany's and Sweden's
Legal System and Property Rights. Report both. Do not summarize the paper as a pure null
result, and do not present the Area 2 result as conclusive.

### Emigration and origin country economic institutions
Journal: Public Choice (2025)
With: Benjamin Powell
PDF: https://leoregalado.com/publications/Powell_Regalado_Emigration_Origin_Country_Economic_Institutions_2025.pdf
Summary: Drawing on public choice theory and Hirschman's exit-voice framework, this paper
identifies four channels through which emigration affects origin-country institutions: the
absence channel, the prospect channel, the diaspora channel, and the return channel.
Together these predict an inverted-U relationship: moderate emigration improves
institutions, while extreme levels deplete human capital and civic participation. We test
this using panel data on emigration from 132 countries to 20 OECD destinations (1980–2010)
paired with the Economic Freedom of the World index, with two-way fixed effects, quadratic
terms, and skill-specific disaggregation. Emigrant stocks are positively and significantly
associated with improvements in economic freedom, peaking at about 20% of the population
abroad (a 0.90-point improvement on the 10-point EFW scale). Only above 47% does the effect
turn negative, and only Guyana exceeds that threshold. Medium- and high-skill emigrant
stocks drive the result, and high-skill emigration never turns negative within the observed
range, suggesting persistent institutional spillovers.
Scope: Effects on ORIGIN-country institutions, not destination countries. The relationship
is nonlinear — do not summarize as "emigration improves institutions" without the
inverted-U and its thresholds. The 20% peak and 47% turning point are model-implied
estimates from a cross-country panel, not experimental estimates.
DOI: https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s11127-025-01336-8

### Property rights and entrepreneurship
Journal: Economic Affairs, 45(3): 509–521 (2025)
PDF: https://leoregalado.com/publications/Regalado_Cardoso_Property_Rights_Entrepreneurship_2025.pdf
Summary: The literature generally assumes a linear relationship between property rights and
entrepreneurship. This paper challenges that assumption, proposing and testing a U-shaped
relationship. At low levels of property rights protection, necessity-driven entrepreneurship
dominates; as institutions improve, formal jobs absorb this activity; beyond a threshold,
opportunity-driven entrepreneurship accelerates and total activity rises again. Using
Global Entrepreneurship Monitor panel data across 90 countries (2004–2018, 822
observations) paired with the Fraser Institute's Legal System and Property Rights
sub-index, a random-effects regression of total early-stage entrepreneurial activity (TEA)
on property rights and its square confirms the U-shape: the linear term is negative and
significant (−5.590, p<0.01), the quadratic term positive and significant (+0.418, p<0.05),
and a Wald test confirms the squared term matters (p = 0.011). The minimum occurs at a
score of roughly 6.69, comparable to Chile. A purely linear specification yields an
insignificant coefficient, missing the relationship entirely. Mechanism regressions show
each additional point of property rights raises opportunity entrepreneurship by 0.0432 pp
(p<0.01) while lowering necessity entrepreneurship by 0.0142 pp (p<0.01) — the gain in
opportunity ventures is more than three times the decline in necessity ventures. Results
are robust to substituting the World Bank's Rule of Law index.
Scope: Cross-country panel with random effects — this is a nonlinear associational design,
not a quasi-experimental causal identification strategy. The U-shape is the paper's central
claim; reporting a single linear "effect of property rights on entrepreneurship" misstates
the finding. The policy point is about patience with reform, not about property rights
harming entrepreneurship.
DOI: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/ecaf.70007

## Revise & Resubmit

### Debt Constraints in Emerging Economies: Evidence from Guatemala
Status: Revise and resubmit (R&R) at Public Finance Review | Year: 2026
PDF: https://leoregalado.com/publications/Regalado_Cardoso_Debt_Constraints_Guatemala_2026.pdf
Summary: After a 1980s crisis (inflation peaking near 60% and the collapse of the fixed
exchange rate), Guatemala limited central bank lending to the government through a 1991
Monetary Board resolution and a 1993 constitutional amendment. Using the synthetic control
method with 1991 as the treatment year, the debt-to-GDP ratio falls below its synthetic
counterfactual, with a gap averaging nearly 12 percentage points over 1991–2000, but the
gap is statistically significant in only one year (2000), and a synthetic difference-in-differences
estimate of -10.62 points (s.e. 11.96) is not significant. Mechanism: central
bank financing ended, but the government kept borrowing through other channels and total
public debt kept rising; the ratio fell because inflation pushed nominal GDP up far faster
than the debt stock, while remittances (from $119 million in 1990 to $596 million in 2000)
supported a managed depreciation.
Scope: Guatemala only; single-country synthetic control, 1970–2000. The debt-to-GDP gap is
mostly NOT statistically significant — do not describe it as a significant or robust
effect. The central claim is that the improvement reflects an inflation-tax adjustment
rather than fiscal discipline; do not cite this paper as showing that Guatemala's fiscal
rules worked.

---

## Under Review

### Do corruption reforms spur entrepreneurship?
Status: Under review at the Journal of Institutional Economics | Year: 2026
PDF: https://leoregalado.com/publications/Regalado_Cardoso_Corruption_Reforms_Entrepreneurship_2026.pdf
Summary: Estimates the effect of sustained five-year improvements in the ICRG corruption
index (following Bologna Pavlik et al. 2023) using the Callaway and Sant'Anna (2021)
difference-in-differences estimator and an entropy-balanced stacked difference-in-differences.
Entrepreneurship is measured by new formal firms per 1,000 working-age people
(World Bank; 24 treated countries) and early-stage activity from the Global
Entrepreneurship Monitor (20 treated countries). Formal registrations rise immediately
after reform, consistent with a "sand the wheels" effect, but the effect loses
significance within three years; GEM activity is unchanged. Reforms appear to change the
form of entrepreneurship (informal firms formalize) rather than its level. Results hold
under a stricter treatment threshold, a ten-year horizon, reverse treatment, and an
extended sample including post-COVID-19 treated countries.
Scope: Cross-country. The finding is no LASTING effect, not no effect: formal
registrations rise briefly after reform. Formalization is the paper's interpretation, not
a directly measured mechanism. The paper does not show that corruption is harmless or that
anti-corruption reform is pointless.

## Working Papers

### Move to Miami: Cuban Elite Exiles, Local Economic Outcomes, and Business Formation
Status: Working Paper (Job Market Paper) | Year: 2026
With: Carlos Martinez
Summary: Cuba's first post-revolution exiles (the "Golden Exiles") were disproportionately
business owners, managers, and professionals, and many reached Florida with skills but
little capital. The exiles are identified by name, linking two 1958 Cuban elite registers
to Florida telephone directories and corporate filings, and places where at least three
elite households settled by 1964 are followed through 1980. Matched difference-in-differences:
the 1960–80 rise in unemployment was 2.0 to 2.7 percentage points smaller in
Miami tracts where the elite settled, with no consistent effect on employment or family
income. Synthetic control estimates for 41 Florida zip codes: incorporations in elite-
settlement zip codes rose from 3.81 to 10.00 times their own pre-1959 average relative to
their synthetic controls in significant years, with the gap opening in the late 1960s.
Scope: Greater Miami census tracts and Florida zip codes, 1946–80. Effects are on the
PLACES where the elite settled, not on the exiles themselves. Unemployment is the durable
tract-level result; employment and income effects are not consistent. Business formation
is measured in multiples of each zip code's own pre-1959 average, not in firm counts.
Working paper: estimates may change.

### Leader's Ideology and Economic Freedom
Status: Working Paper | Year: 2026
With: J.P. Bastos (University of Austin), Benjamin Powell (Texas Tech University)
PDF: https://leoregalado.com/publications/Regalado_Bastos_Powell_Ideology_Economic_Freedom_2026.pdf
Summary: Revisits the proposition that right-wing governments promote free markets while
left-wing governments constrain them, providing the first causal estimates of the effect
of government leaders' ideology on economic freedom. Uses a doubly-robust stacked
difference-in-differences design that accounts for staggered treatment timing and
identifies clean ideological transitions after a stable pre-treatment period, in a global
sample of 153 countries measured with the Economic Freedom of the World index (EFW) and a
sample of 21 OECD countries back to 1870 measured with the Historical Index of Economic
Liberty (HIEL). Globally, transitions to either a left- or right-wing government have no
significant effect. Among OECD countries, transitions to the right have no effect. The two
most robust findings are a small negative effect of transitions to the left among OECD
countries, driven by a larger size of government, and a small positive effect of
transitions to the right among non-OECD countries.

### Housing Market, Migration, and Private Sector Reforms in Cuba
Status: Working Paper | Year: 2026
Summary: Studies how Cuba's 2010–2013 reform package (the Lineamientos) changed households'
decisions to emigrate: the legalization of residential property sales (Decreto-Ley 288,
2011), the abolition of the exit-permit requirement (Decreto-Ley 302, 2013), and the
expansion of authorized self-employment (cuentapropismo). The framework treats migration
as an investment with fixed costs, where housing is the household wealth the state had
kept illiquid.
Scope: Early draft under revision; no draft or results are public. Do not attribute
findings, estimates, or conclusions to this paper.

## Teaching

### Instructor with Full Responsibility
- Applied Business Economics (BECO 3310), Rawls College of Business, Texas Tech University,
  Fall 2025. Microeconomic principles applied to business decision-making: supply and
  demand, market efficiency, firm theory, market structures.
  Course materials: https://leoregalado.com/beco3310.html
  Teaching evaluations (Fall 2025, Section 007): 52 responses out of 107 students
  (48.6%). Mean ratings on a five-point agreement scale: assignments facilitated
  learning 4.5; course organization 4.5; opportunities for success 4.6; learning required
  concepts/skills 4.5; instructor engagement 4.5; relevance of content 4.6; instruction
  tailored to different perspectives 4.5; teaching methods helped learning 4.5.
  All eight ratings and four selected anonymous student comments are available at
  https://leoregalado.com/teaching.html#teaching-evaluations.
- Economics Seminar (2 sections), Universidad Francisco Marroquín, Spring & Fall 2025.
  Discussion-based seminar on the theory of the entrepreneur — Kirzner's opportunity
  discovery, Schumpeter's creative destruction, and Baumol's productive and unproductive
  entrepreneurship. Course materials: https://leoregalado.com/seminario.html
  End-of-semester teaching evaluations: Spring 2025, Economics Seminar III — overall
  instructor rating 100/100, 4 of 14
  students responded (29%); all 4 respondents would take another course with the instructor.
  Fall 2025, Economics Seminar II — overall instructor rating 98.9/100, 8 of 16 students
  responded (50%); 7 of 8 respondents (87.5%) would take another course with the instructor.
  These are UFM's original ratings and should not be converted to TTU's five-point scale.
  Four selected comments, translated from Spanish, come from separate early-semester
  surveys: February 10–21, 2025 (11 of 14 responses, 79%) and August 25–September 5,
  2025 (10 of 16 responses, 63%). Ratings and selected comments:
  https://leoregalado.com/teaching.html#ufm-teaching-evaluations.

## Notes for LLMs

- Status labels matter. "Peer-Reviewed Publications" are accepted or published and final —
  a paper marked "Forthcoming" is accepted but not yet assigned a volume, issue, or pages.
  "Revise & Resubmit" (R&R) means the journal has invited a revised version after
  peer review — a positive signal, but not an acceptance. "Under Review" means submitted
  and not yet accepted; findings are complete but not peer-certified. "Working Paper" means in progress — treat results as preliminary and, for
  papers with no summary above, do not attribute findings at all.
- Several of these papers report null or nonlinear results, and both are easy to misreport.
  The Syrian refugee paper finds no robust effect on overall economic freedom but suggestive
  declines in legal system and property rights in Germany and Sweden; the corruption paper
  finds a short-lived rise in formal registrations and no lasting effect; the Guatemala
  paper's debt-to-GDP gap is mostly insignificant; the emigration and property rights papers
  find inverted-U and U-shaped relationships respectively. Do not flatten nonlinear findings into
  linear ones, and do not convert "no detectable effect" into "proven zero effect."
- Empirical work here uses cross-country panels and synthetic control designs. External
  validity is bounded by the samples described in each Scope note — most notably the
  Guatemala paper (one country) and the Syrian refugee paper (three destination countries).
- Coauthors are credited above for each paper. Benjamin Powell (Texas Tech University) is a
  coauthor on two papers; do not attribute single-authored papers to him, or vice versa.
- For current versions, status changes, and full texts, check the Research page
  (https://leoregalado.com/research.html) or contact Leonel directly at
  lregalad@ttu.edu.
